title: Stand like an anvil (Ignatius to Polycarp 3)
hook: stand firm as an anvil under the hammer
tomorrow: why would a bishop shout "away with the atheists"?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius writing ahead to the church in Rome, asking them not to stand in his way, and calling himself God's wheat. The line was god's wheat.

The family group chat hasn't stopped since breakfast. Every message lands like a hammer: you should, you never, why can't you. Some weeks the pressure comes exactly like that, blow after blow, and you can feel yourself starting to bend. A man in chains knew the feeling. Ignatius, the same prisoner from yesterday, is being taken under guard toward Rome. On the way he stops long enough to write to a friend, Polycarp, a bishop with hammers of his own coming. What do you tell a friend when you may never write to him again?
screen: `THE CHAT THAT WON'T STOP.` → `A PRISONER WRITES TO A FRIEND.` → `WHAT DO YOU TELL HIM?`

segments.voice: Ignatius doesn't send a pep talk. He sends a picture. First, the hammers. In chapter three he warns Polycarp about people who seem trustworthy but teach strange things. Don't let them shake you, he says. Second, the anvil. Stand firm, like an anvil when it's struck. Think about what an anvil does in a blacksmith's shop. It doesn't dodge the hammer, and it doesn't swing back. It stays, and the hot iron gets shaped on top of it. Third, the athlete. Ignatius switches pictures in the same breath: it belongs to a great athlete to take the blows and still win. The win isn't avoiding the hits. It's still standing at the end. Then he adds the reason: for God's sake we put up with everything, so that God will put up with us. Fourth, where to look. Ignatius tells his friend to watch the times, and to wait for the one who is above all time, the unseen one who became visible for our sake. That's where the steadiness comes from. Not from being hard, but from looking past the hammer. And the detail to tell a friend tonight: the man who received this letter, Polycarp of Smyrna, would one day need every word of it.
screen: `DON'T LET THEM SHAKE YOU.` · `STAND LIKE A STRUCK ANVIL.` · `THE ATHLETE TAKES BLOWS AND WINS.` · `LOOK TO THE ONE ABOVE TIME.` · then, large: `AN ANVIL.`

segments.voice: Stand up, feet flat and a little apart, knees soft, the way an anvil sits on its block. Bring one pressure to mind, just one: a deadline, a person, a voice in your own head. Let it land, breath after breath, and stay right where you are.
Stand like an anvil. Ignatius's advice to a friend under pressure: take the blows without swinging back, and stay.
Your line: an anvil. Struck all day, and still there when the hammer stops. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep feast days for both Ignatius of Antioch and Polycarp, and passages from Ignatius's letters are read in the Church's Liturgy of the Hours.

fork.setup: your manager keeps moving your shifts and hinting you're not committed. one coworker says quit, another says blow up at him. what does the anvil do?

fork.reveal: Ignatius's anvil neither dodges nor strikes back. it stays put while the blows land, and for him the steadiness came from looking past the hammer to God.

chat.meaning: Ignatius tells Polycarp to stand like a struck anvil: it takes the blows without swinging back or running, and stays.

anvil.meaning: the heavy iron block a blacksmith hammers metal on

notes: Letter to Polycarp 3 paraphrased (Lightfoot 1891 is public domain, but the exact wording wasn't certain enough to quote). Confirm: don't be dismayed by plausible men who teach strange doctrine; stand firm as an anvil when it is struck; it is the part of a great athlete to receive blows and win; for God's sake we must endure all things so that he may endure us; mark the times; await him who is above time, invisible, who became visible for our sake.
The description of what an anvil does in a blacksmith's shop is the writer's gloss on the image, not Ignatius's words.
'Taken under guard toward Rome' leans on yesterday's Letter to the Romans; no date, age or number of guards is given (claims rule).
'Would one day need every word of it' points to tomorrow's Martyrdom of Polycarp without giving his age or a date.
